profiles.meeting_scenario: In February 2009, a USGS GeoMAC archive coordinator and a Geographic Area Coordination Center GIS liaison meet to coordinate the handoff of the 2008 historic wildland fire perimeter archive. The source perimeters have already been gathered from incident intelligence, GPS, and infrared imagery and normalized into GeoMAC workflows, but the two workstreams need to align on what is considered ready to move from operational holdings into the year/state historical archive. Their agenda is to confirm the California and Nevada handoff, verify which 2008 incident versions belong in the annual release, make sure the data have 'passed validation' before loading, and confirm that the deliverables will arrive in the 'standard GeoMAC export format' for posting to the RMGSC historic_fire_data site. The expected outcome is an apparently straightforward agreement that the liaison will send the 2008 state deliverables and the archive coordinator will load and publish them without further clarification.

members.name: Dana Holt
members.expertise: Geospatial data standardization, historical archive publishing, GeoMAC database loading, release packaging
members.background: Dana works at the Rocky Mountain Geographic Science Center and manages the back end of annual GeoMAC historical releases, including schema normalization, archive folder structure, state/year packaging, and public download publication.
members.private_state: Dana wants to post the 2008 archive on schedule with minimal back-and-forth, avoid reopening incident-level questions, and keep the release consistent with prior-year archive conventions so downstream users see a stable historical product.
hidden_assumptions: A 'final perimeter' for the 2008 archive is the last perimeter that belongs to the 2008 archive cycle, effectively the last accepted 2008 snapshot rather than a later closeout revision.
The 'California package' means incidents filed under California in the archive's state-based organization, not incidents grouped by the coordination path used during the season.

If data have 'passed validation' or are 'ready for loading,' that means they satisfy archive-entry checks such as field conformity, geometry/topology cleanliness, naming consistency, and absence of publication blockers.

The 'standard GeoMAC export format' in a handoff context means the archive-ready state publication bundle used for the historical download site, even if the same phrase is used differently in operational contexts.

members.name: Luis Romero
members.expertise: Incident perimeter compilation, regional fire intelligence support, IR/GPS reconciliation, operational GIS handoffs
members.background: Luis supports wildfire incident GIS coordination across the California/Nevada operations area, consolidating perimeter updates from incident teams and ensuring that operationally trusted versions are available to GeoMAC and partner agencies.
members.private_state: Luis wants the 2008 archive to reflect the most incident-trustworthy perimeter versions without spending extra time reformatting data, and he wants border incidents to remain discoverable in the same organizational pattern field users remember from the season.
hidden_assumptions: A 'final perimeter' is the incident-approved contained or closeout perimeter for a 2008 fire, even if that vetted version was transmitted in early 2009.
The 'California package' means the California-side operational set that users followed during the season, including some border or multi-state incidents handled through California coordination.

If a perimeter set has 'passed validation' or is 'ready for loading,' that means the meaningful content checks are done: major fires were reconciled against IR flights, GPS traces, and incident intelligence notes well enough to trust the boundaries.

The 'standard GeoMAC export format' refers to the familiar GeoMAC-style outputs people already exchange and inspect from the web/application side, especially per-incident exports that preserve the operational viewing pattern.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'final perimeter' for a 2008 fire
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to sending and publishing the 'final perimeter' for each 2008 incident.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the latest perimeter snapshot that belongs inside the 2008 archive cutoff, even if a later closeout version exists after year-end.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the incident team's closeout or contained perimeter, even if that vetted version arrived in January 2009 for a 2008 fire.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'final perimeter' sounds like a settled domain term, and both participants have legitimate professional reasons to treat their interpretation as the obvious one; because they are discussing routine handoff rather than incident adjudication, neither expects the calendar-year versus incident-lifecycle distinction to need restating.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the 'California package' as though it names a single obvious deliverable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the archive package for incidents assigned to California in the historical state-based archive structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the California-side operational package, including incidents users associated with California coordination even when the archive state assignment is Nevada or multi-state.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The deliverable label is familiar and concrete enough to create false confidence, and the mismatch only affects edge cases like border fires, so both parties treat the phrase as already precise without realizing they are indexing different grouping logics.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the 2008 perimeter set has 'passed validation' and will be 'ready for loading.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the package has cleared archive-ingest criteria: standardized fields, valid geometry, consistent naming, and no structural issues that would block loading or public release.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the perimeter content has been sufficiently checked against source evidence such as IR imagery, GPS, and incident intelligence notes so the fire boundaries are trustworthy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Unlike a formal checklist term such as 'QA complete,' 'passed validation' and 'ready for loading' are naturally used as workflow shorthand in both operational and archival contexts; each participant hears a familiar gate being reported and assumes it refers to the relevant validation gate in their own stream.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'standard GeoMAC export format'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the handoff will come in the 'standard GeoMAC export format' for shapefile and KML posting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the archive-standard export: a state-year publication bundle arranged for the historic download site.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the operationally standard GeoMAC-style export people are used to handling from the application side, especially per-incident shapefile/KML outputs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds highly specific and institutionally shared, which makes clarification feel unnecessary, but 'standard' quietly points to different local standards on each side; because both agree on file formats and overall purpose, the packaging procedure remains invisible during the meeting.

For this handoff, I mean California and Nevada as they exist in the state-based archive structure, and the final perimeter is whatever belongs in the 2008 archive cycle. If Luis confirms the normal package state, I can keep the posting schedule and stay consistent with prior-year releases.

turns.utterance: That's fine. I'll send the standard GeoMAC export format we've been using, and it's easy for my team to spot-check before release.

turns.inner_thought: Once I ingest this, it becomes the stable 2008 archive snapshot, and I do not want to revisit incident-level revisions afterward. Ready for loading means archive-ready to publish, and final perimeter means the last accepted 2008 snapshot for the annual release.
turns.utterance: Great. Once the files are ready for loading, I'll treat them as the stable 2008 archive snapshot and take over the archive-side posting.
